content: The MenAfriVac vaccine had not yet been introduced. During NmW and NmX epidemics, approximately 9% of cases were attributed to Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) or Streptococcus pneumoniae (Spn), compared to about 13% in NmA epidemics. However, the confidence intervals were wide, and the differences were not statistically significant. Despite this, the lower proportion of cases caused by Spn or Hib in NmW and NmX epidemics is unexpected, given the higher proportion of Spn cases observed in the meningitis belt in recent years. The distribution of pathogens by age group was similar between NmW/NmX and NmA epidemics. However, comparisons of age group distribution for NmA epidemics were limited to data from one country, with small sample sizes in many age categories. In NmW epidemics, the proportion of other pathogens in children aged 2–14 years was 5%, increasing to 9% in individuals aged 15–29 years, and was higher in those over 29 years of age. The quality of evidence was considered very low due to variability between studies, changes in vaccination programs affecting pathogen distribution, and potential bias toward reporting findings from larger epidemics. For bacterial meningitis caused by pathogens such as Spn or Hib, antibiotic treatment for 10–14 days (and at least 5 days) is typically recommended for presumptive treatment of acute bacterial meningitis. Meningitis caused by Spn or Hib carries a higher risk of complications and mortality compared to meningococcal meningitis, suggesting that longer treatment durations may reduce morbidity and mortality. Evidence suggests that the proportion of Hib and Spn meningitis cases may be similar across NmW, NmX, and NmA epidemics. Therefore, during outbreaks, up to 8% of cases (those caused by Hib or Spn) may receive suboptimal treatment if shorter antibiotic regimens are used. Conversely, inappropriate short-term treatment may increase the risk of antibiotic resistance. There is also a growing trend of resistance to chloramphenicol among Nm, Spn, and Hib. The cost of a 5-day course of ceftriaxone is approximately USD $7, excluding hospitalization costs, which adds an economic burden to families and health services. If all meningitis cases, including 90% of meningococcal meningitis cases, are treated with a 5-day regimen during epidemics, the number of hospital bed days required could be three to four times higher than with a single-dose treatment policy. However, hospitalization is not mandatory if the patient is stable and can return daily for antibiotics. The increased care costs must be weighed against the potential costs of higher morbidity and mortality associated with single-dose treatment policies. For families, longer treatment regimens may be acceptable if governments ensure free treatment during epidemics, as per current policy. The Guideline Development Group concluded that the benefits of adopting longer antibiotic treatment regimens as standard treatment—recently reviewed for children—outweigh the potential adverse effects and higher costs, given the higher case fatality and complications associated with Hib and Spn meningitis. In large-scale NmA epidemics, where meningococcal cases overwhelmed health centers, a single-dose treatment policy followed by longer treatment if the patient did not improve was deemed appropriate. With fewer meningococcal meningitis epidemics and smaller outbreaks following the introduction of MenAfriVac, implementing longer treatment regimens should be more feasible. The question remains whether single-dose antibiotic regimens should continue to be recommended for suspected meningitis cases during meningococcal meningitis outbreaks, and if so, under what circumstances. Recommendations now suggest that suspected bacterial meningitis cases in children under 2 months should be treated with a 7-day course of ceftriaxone, while those aged 2 months and older should receive a 5-day course. Single-dose antibiotic treatment is no longer recommended. In large-scale epidemics in remote areas or regions with weak infrastructure, single-dose treatment protocols may still be implemented if the epidemic is confirmed to be caused by meningococcus. In such cases, single-dose ceftriaxone should be used with follow-up at 24 and 48 hours. Oily chloramphenicol is advised only as an alternative where ceftriaxone is unavailable or inappropriate. The constant threat of emerging antibiotic resistance must be closely monitored to ensure that recommended antibiotic regimens remain appropriate and are adapted as necessary. Maintaining a policy of free treatment during meningococcal meningitis epidemics is crucial, with cost implications for government health services. Compliance with recommended treatment protocols and outcomes (morbidity and mortality) should be monitored and evaluated. In the search for systematic reviews, 906 records were identified, of which four met the inclusion criteria. One review met the quality criteria for chemoprophylaxis, but none met the criteria for early vaccination of household contacts. In a subsequent search for primary articles, 2,936 records were identified, with two papers meeting the inclusion criteria: one on chemoprophylaxis and the other on vaccination. Evidence of the benefit of chemoprophylaxis (four observational studies) and vaccination (one quasi-randomized trial) on the risk of subsequent meningococcal disease among household contacts is limited. Using pooled estimates, 200 household contacts would need to be treated to prevent one case of meningococcal disease. The quality of evidence was assessed as very low due to the observational nature of the studies, small sample sizes, and lack of studies from the African meningitis belt. In industrialized countries, the relative risk of meningococcal disease among household contacts often reaches 1,200–1,400 in non-outbreak situations. Low-income families may be at higher risk for meningitis and could benefit from effective prophylaxis, but detection and response capacity vary, and small communities may be disadvantaged. Side effects of commonly recommended antibiotics (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, and ceftriaxone) and meningococcal vaccines are generally mild, but the development of antibiotic resistance is a global public health threat. Rifampicin use can lead to resistance among meningococci and may not be acceptable in meningitis belt countries due to its importance in tuberculosis treatment. Any exposure to antibiotics generates a risk of developing resistance in bacteria from the digestive, cutaneous, and nasal flora. The cost of antibiotic treatment per 100 contacts treated is approximately USD $48 for rifampicin, USD $50 for ceftriaxone, USD $4 for ciprofloxacin, and USD $44 for azithromycin. The cost per 100 people vaccinated is USD $60 for MenAfriVac and USD $250 for ACW vaccine. Costs of stocking and distributing vaccines must also be considered, as well as the challenges of managing vaccine supply for relatively small quantities. Antibiotic prophylaxis is currently recommended for household contacts of those with sporadic invasive meningococcal disease but not for widespread use or administration to household contacts during epidemics. Before an epidemic is declared, this policy should be applied to affected families. The Guideline Development Group agreed that while the benefit of antibiotic prophylaxis in the meningitis belt is uncertain, the low cost and risk of adverse effects of single-dose ciprofloxacin may make it beneficial even if the absolute benefit is small. However, no new information suggests that chemoprophylaxis for household contacts during epidemics would offer additional community benefits when case management and vaccination programs are in place. For vaccination as a household prophylactic measure ahead of mass vaccination, the group considered that any additional benefit would be small relative to the difficulties of implementation, particularly where mass vaccination is planned for the community. The administration of prophylaxis to household contacts implies a need to confirm meningococcal meningitis cases promptly. Recommendations on dosage, route of administration, and contraindications will be made available to countries. The effectiveness of this intervention would be best evaluated in a randomized trial. However, the logistical challenges of conducting a trial across districts and countries with a sufficient sample size of cases in household contacts outside epidemics may be prohibitively large. A summary of the guideline will be published in the Weekly Epidemiological Record in English and French. The guideline will also be published in English, and findings from systematic reviews and retrospective data analysis will be submitted to peer-reviewed scientific journals. The reference guide Managing meningitis epidemics in Africa will be revised and widely distributed to those in charge of meningitis outbreak response. Recommendations in other WHO guidance documents will be revised or replaced as necessary. Web-based documents presenting recommendations will be updated or archived. The recommendations will be presented at the annual WHO inter-country meeting on surveillance and response to meningitis epidemics in Africa, as well as other meetings, workshops, and training sessions. Links to the guideline will be placed on the department website and shared with WHO partners, regional and country offices, collaborating centers, relevant ministries of health, NGOs, vaccine and antibiotic manufacturers, and funding agencies. The implementation of these updated recommendations will be assessed through consultations with ministries, feedback at the annual WHO inter-country meeting, and evaluation of meningitis data reported to the Inter-country Support Team in Ouagadougou. The guideline will be reviewed by WHO within five years of publication. The difficulty of reaching clear evidence-based recommendations on reactive vaccination policies with polysaccharide vaccines highlights the importance of advancing the development and introduction of polyvalent conjugate vaccines.
